definition: HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS) is an encrypted version of HTTP that uses SSL/TLS encryption to secure data transmission between your browser and websites.
metaDescription: HTTPS encrypts data between your browser and websites, protecting against eavesdropping and tampering. Learn why the padlock icon matters for privacy.
simpleExplanation: HTTPS is like sending mail in a locked box instead of a postcard. When you visit a website with HTTPS (look for the padlock icon), all information you send and receive is encrypted, making it unreadable to anyone trying to intercept it.
whyItMatters: HTTPS protects your passwords, personal information, and browsing activity from being intercepted by hackers, especially on public Wi-Fi. It also verifies you're connecting to the real website, not a fake one designed to steal your data.
technicalDetail: HTTPS uses SSL/TLS protocols to create an encrypted tunnel between client and server. It provides confidentiality through encryption, integrity through message authentication codes, and authenticity through digital certificates issued by trusted Certificate Authorities.

examples.explanation: When you log into your bank account, HTTPS encrypts your username, password, and account information so hackers can't steal your credentials even if they intercept the data.
HTTPS protects your credit card details and personal information when making purchases, ensuring the data can't be read by cybercriminals on the same network.
On coffee shop Wi-Fi, HTTPS prevents other users from seeing what websites you visit or intercepting any forms you fill out, even though you're on an unsecured network.
